title: Hypnos: Learning Generalisable Representations of Sleep Physiology via Next-Token Prediction
claim: Tokenize each sensor modality, group modalities for next-token prediction, then reuse the learned embeddings across varied sensor subsets and downstream tasks.
layout: 2 sections, left-to-right; pre-training stages then evaluation tasks, arrows between stages
description: A wide horizontal figure split into 'Pre-training' (left) and 'Evaluation' (right) by a vertical line. At far left, five physiological modalities (EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG, Resp) are shown with body-part icons and raw waveform traces. A grey arrow leads to a dashed box with a grid of colored squares, one row per modality, labeled 'Tokenization', with ellipses for sequence length. Another arrow leads to a 'Modality grouping' box, where the rows are split into dashed sub-groups and linked by vertical lines to show restricted cross-modal attention. A third arrow leads to 'Next-token prediction', a column of faded, dashed target tokens. The evaluation side shows nested ovals with icons for different sensor subsets. These ovals lead to three task panels: sleep staging (hypnogram), cortical arousal detection (EEG trace), and condition classification (Afib ECG, apnoea respiration trace).
caption: Overview. Hypnos is a large auto-regressive RQ-transformer trained via multi-modal next-token prediction on tokenized streams of physiological sensor data. During pre-training, cross-modal attention is restricted to randomly sampled sub-groups, improving test-time generalisation to subsets of supported modalities. After pre-training, Hypnos can be used to generate high-quality embeddings for a diverse range of sensor configurations and downstream tasks over different timescales. We evaluate on tasks including sleep stage classification of overnight recordings, the detection of cortical arousal events, and atrial fibrillation (Afib) detection.
abstract: Foundation models offer a promising route to compress multi-modal physiological signals into compact representations of human health, with broad applications across sleep medicine, cardiology, neurology and other healthcare domains. Existing models have typically been trained with masked-reconstruction or contrastive objectives. However, masked reconstruction may be poorly suited to the stochastic nature of these signals, while contrastive approaches rely on positive-pair definitions despite the semantic invariances of physiological signals being poorly understood. In this work, we show that next-token prediction is a simple and scalable alternative. We develop Hypnos, a multi-modal sleep foundation model trained using eight different sensing modalities (e.g. EEG, ECG, respiratory signals) drawn from over 20{,}000 overnight polysomnography recordings. We tokenize each modality into streams of discrete tokens using residual vector quantization, then train a large auto-regressive RQ-Transformer to jointly predict the next token across all modalities in parallel. After training, Hypnos can be applied to continuous streams of sensor data from any subset of supported modalities, generating embeddings for downstream tasks. Hypnos significantly outperforms existing foundation models on most benchmarks evaluated. In sleep stage classification, we match the performance of strong supervised baselines on held-out test sets whilst using 100\times less labelled data. Hypnos even generalises beyond sleep recordings, surpassing a dedicated ECG foundation model at detecting atrial fibrillation. Our results demonstrate that auto-regressive token modelling is a strong self-supervised approach for representation learning from multi-modal physiological signals. Code and model weights: https://github.com/joncarter1/hypnos
